explanations.explanation: God is the one. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says, “Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children…” (Ephesians 5:1). The pattern isn't a hero down the street. It's the Father Himself, and beloved children get to copy Him.

Paul is the apostle writing this letter, and he doesn't point at himself. He points higher: “Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children…” (Ephesians 5:1). Plenty of writers would slip their own name in as the pattern. Paul tells the believers to imitate God.

The apostles aren't named in this verse at all. Paul, the apostle writing the letter, says, “Be imitators of God…” (Ephesians 5:1). As a stamper, I can tell you the pattern matters more than whoever is holding the handle. Here the pattern is God.

explanations.answer: Christ giving Himself up for us
explanations.explanation: That's the picture. Paul says to walk in love, “…just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.” (Ephesians 5:2). The love he's pointing to is the love Christ already showed. Paul didn't have to go looking for an example.

explanations.answer: God forgiving Israel again and again
explanations.explanation: That isn't what this verse points to. Paul sends the believers to one picture in verse 2: Christ, who “…loved us and gave Himself up for us…” He doesn't mention Israel here. The example is Christ, and it's right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: The church sharing all it had
explanations.explanation: Sharing is a fine thing, but it isn't the picture Paul uses here. He says to walk in love “…just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us…” (Ephesians 5:2). The measuring stick is Christ's love. That one is plenty to keep a person busy for a lifetime.

Paul doesn't leave any room for a little. He says, “…there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed.” (Ephesians 5:3). Not even a hint, baker. So a small greed doesn't get a pass, and it can't slip in just because it's tiny.

Right, the text says the opposite. Paul writes, “…there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed.” (Ephesians 5:3). Greed is on that list with no size limit. Not even a hint means not even a hint, and I couldn't say it better.

He sure does. Paul writes, “Nor should there be obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking, which are out of character, but rather thanksgiving.” (Ephesians 5:4). Out of character means it doesn't fit who these believers are. And look at what he puts in its place: thanksgiving.

The text says exactly that. Paul writes, “Nor should there be obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking, which are out of character, but rather thanksgiving.” (Ephesians 5:4). Out of character is his phrase for all three. I joke all day long, friend, so I'm glad there's a clean way to do it, and thanksgiving is right in the verse.

The verse says the opposite. Paul writes, “For of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” (Ephesians 5:5). He opens with “…you can be sure…” so he isn't leaving this one open to guesses. Nothing about it is vague.

That's the answer: False. Paul writes, “For of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” (Ephesians 5:5). He opens with “…you can be sure…” so there's nothing here to haggle over. I've tried haggling with my oven timer, and it never works either.

Yes, that's the note. The verse says “…(that is, an idolater)…” right after the words about the greedy person. Paul ties greed to idolatry in that one little aside. It's a short note, but it packs a lot in.

No coward in this verse, friend, and I'm not judging, because I once spent a whole afternoon hunting for a spatula I was holding in my mustache. The note says the greedy person is an idolater. It sits in the verse that says no immoral, impure, or greedy person has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God (Ephesians 5:5). So greed isn't treated as a small habit here. It's listed in serious company.

Liar is a good guess, but it isn't in this verse. The note says the greedy person is an idolater. The verse says no immoral, impure, or greedy person has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God (Ephesians 5:5). So Paul puts greed on the same serious list as the other two, and the note is what makes that stand out.

That's it. Paul says, “Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.” (Ephesians 5:6). He warns against being deceived with empty words, and then he names what is coming. It's the wrath of God.

A famine isn't in this verse. Paul says, “…because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.” (Ephesians 5:6). The thing coming is the wrath of God, and that's all the verse says about it. Empty words can't change that.

No army shows up in this verse. Paul says, “…because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.” (Ephesians 5:6). The wrath of God is the thing he names. Nobody marches in, so there's no army to look for.

Paul says the opposite. His words are, “Therefore do not be partakers with them.” (Ephesians 5:7). He doesn't tell the believers to join in with the sons of disobedience. And he doesn't give a win-them-over plan in this verse, so I won't make one up either.

That's right, and the verse is short and clear: “Therefore do not be partakers with them.” (Ephesians 5:7). Paul never says to join them. He says not to be partakers with them, and he leaves it at that. Short verse, big point.

That's the one. Paul says, “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light…” (Ephesians 5:8). Notice the order: he tells them what they are before he tells them how to walk. The walk follows the light.

Strangers in the land isn't in this verse. Paul says, “Walk as children of light…” (Ephesians 5:8). He's just told them they are now “…light in the Lord.” so the walk matches the light. It's about who they are, not about where they are.

Soldiers on guard isn't what the verse says. Paul says, “Walk as children of light…” (Ephesians 5:8). He's just said they are “…light in the Lord.” and the walk fits that. Children of light is the phrase to hold onto.

Close, but the verse says someone else. Paul writes, “Test and prove what pleases the Lord.” (Ephesians 5:10). It isn't about pleasing other people. Pleasing everybody sounds like a full-time job, and I'd end up as crumbs.

Right, it's not about pleasing other people. Paul says, “Test and prove what pleases the Lord.” (Ephesians 5:10). The Lord is the one whose pleasure the children of light are trying to learn. That's a much better aim than guessing what a crowd wants.

Expose is the word. Paul says, “Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them.” (Ephesians 5:11). Children of light don't join in, and they don't just look away either. The light does its work by showing things as they are.

Ignore isn't the word. Paul says, “Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them.” (Ephesians 5:11). Staying out of it is half of it. The other half is the word “expose.”

Excuse isn't the word. Paul says, “Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them.” (Ephesians 5:11). Making excuses is the opposite of what the verse asks. The word he picks is “expose.”

Yes, he does. Paul writes, “…everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself.” (Ephesians 5:13). The light doesn't just show things, it says what it shines on becomes light too. True is the answer, baker.

The verse says it does. Paul writes, “But everything exposed by the light becomes visible, for everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself.” (Ephesians 5:13). So the light makes things visible, and what it shines on becomes light itself. That makes True the answer.

explanations.answer: Christ will shine on the sleeper
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. The saying goes, “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” (Ephesians 5:14). It tells the sleeper to wake up and rise, and it says Christ will shine on him. Paul introduces it with “So it is said…” so he's passing along a saying.

Rest isn't what the saying promises. It goes, “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” (Ephesians 5:14). The sleeper is being told to wake up, not to settle in. What follows is that Christ will shine on him.

No enemies show up in the saying. It goes, “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” (Ephesians 5:14). What comes after the waking is Christ shining on the sleeper. That's the whole promise.
The verse says the opposite. Paul writes, “…redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” (Ephesians 5:16). He calls the days evil, not good. It's a reason to make good use of the time.
That's right. Paul writes, “…redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” (Ephesians 5:16). He calls the days evil, and that's why the time matters. Good call, baker.

Lord's is it. Paul says, “Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.” (Ephesians 5:17). The opposite of foolish here is understanding the Lord's will. That's the thing to chase.

The world's will isn't in this verse. Paul says, “Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.” (Ephesians 5:17). It's the Lord's will that he wants them to understand. He sets that against being foolish.

The elders aren't in this verse. Paul says, “Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.” (Ephesians 5:17). The will to understand belongs to the Lord. It's a quick fill-in, but it's the whole point.

Yes, the Spirit. Paul says, “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18). He warns against getting drunk on wine, and the one to be filled with is the Spirit. Notice he doesn't just say stop. He says what to take up instead.

The Law isn't what he says here. Paul says, “Instead, be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18). That comes right after the line about getting drunk on wine. The Spirit is the one to be filled with.
Good deeds aren't the answer in this verse. Paul says, “Instead, be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18). That's what comes after the warning about wine. Being filled is about the Spirit.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, “Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.” (Ephesians 5:19). So they're meant to be shared, not kept to yourself. A song in the heart is good, but it's also meant to go out to the people next to you.

Right, they aren't kept to yourself. Paul writes, “Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord…” (Ephesians 5:19). It's both: to one another and in your hearts to the Lord. Nobody in that verse is asked to sing solo in a closet.

Always is the word. Paul says, “…always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” (Ephesians 5:20). Not now and then, but always, and for everything. That's a thankful way to live.

Every morning is a nice habit, but it isn't what the verse says. Paul says, “…always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” (Ephesians 5:20). The word is “always,” which covers mornings and every other hour too.

Every Sabbath isn't the word in this verse. Paul says, “…always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” (Ephesians 5:20). It's “always,” not one day a week. That leaves no day out.
